clinicalPearls: Characterised by agitation, tachycardia, hypertension, hyperthermia, dilated pupils and prominent sweating
Typical causes include cocaine, amphetamines and related stimulants and some decongestants
The presence of sweating and usually preserved bowel sounds distinguishes it from the dry anticholinergic toxidrome
Benzodiazepines are the cornerstone of treatment, controlling agitation, tachycardia and hypertension
Complications include seizures, myocardial ischaemia, hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis and intracranial haemorrhage
Traditional teaching cautions against beta-blocker monotherapy in cocaine toxicity because of concern about unopposed alpha stimulation
reference.pathophysiology: The sympathomimetic toxidrome results from excessive stimulation of adrenergic receptors through increased release or reduced reuptake of catecholamines, or direct receptor agonism. The resulting adrenergic overdrive raises heart rate, blood pressure and temperature, dilates pupils and stimulates sweating, while central stimulation causes agitation and can provoke seizures. End-organ complications arise from vasoconstriction and increased metabolic demand, including myocardial ischaemia, cerebral haemorrhage and hyperthermia with rhabdomyolysis.
additionalInvestigations: Clinical recognition and a substance-use history
Electrocardiogram and cardiac assessment for ischaemia and arrhythmia
Temperature, creatine kinase and renal function for hyperthermia and rhabdomyolysis
Neuroimaging if focal signs or severe headache suggest intracranial haemorrhage
Glucose and electrolytes to exclude mimics
redFlags: Chest pain or electrocardiographic evidence of ischaemia
reference.prognosis: Most patients recover with sedation and supportive care, but severe hyperthermia, myocardial infarction, intracranial haemorrhage or status epilepticus can be fatal.
pitfalls: Confusing it with the anticholinergic toxidrome (sweaty versus dry skin)
Under-sedating agitated patients and allowing hyperthermia to progress
Overlooking myocardial ischaemia or intracranial haemorrhage
Giving beta-blocker monotherapy in cocaine toxicity against traditional caution
management: Give benzodiazepines as first-line treatment to control agitation, tachycardia, hypertension and seizures
Treat significant hyperthermia with rapid external cooling and manage rhabdomyolysis with intravenous fluids

Control persistent hypertension or myocardial ischaemia with vasodilators such as nitrates or phentolamine, avoiding beta-blocker monotherapy in suspected cocaine toxicity because of unopposed alpha stimulation
Provide supportive care with cardiac monitoring and correction of glucose and electrolyte abnormalities
Consider gastrointestinal decontamination for recent oral ingestion or drug body-packing
Investigate and treat complications including seizures, arrhythmia and intracranial haemorrhage
Involve a clinical toxicology or poisons service for guidance in severe cases
